questions.prompt: What does the height of a bar show?
options: The count or value for that category
The average of the whole chart
questions.explanation: Each bar's height represents that category's count on the value axis.
questions.misconception: Height is the value, not order or color — the average in the whole chart would be one line, not per-bar heights.

questions.prompt: The side axis of a bar chart shows...
questions.explanation: The value axis (vertical) measures the counts each bar reaches.
questions.misconception: The categories line up on the bottom axis — the side axis measures how high each bar, i.e. the value.

questions.prompt: How do you read the value of a bar?
options: Run a line from its top to the value axis
Read the label under the bar only
Look at the tallest bar's color
questions.explanation: Read across from the bar top to the number on the value axis.
questions.misconception: The label names the category but not the value — the height itself projects onto the value axis.

questions.prompt: How can you tell which category is biggest at a glance?
options: The bar with the lighter color
The first bar on the left
The bar with the widest space
questions.explanation: The tallest bar is the biggest category — heights make comparison instant.
questions.misconception: Color, position, and spacing carry no value — height is the only measure here.

questions.prompt: When is a bar chart the better choice than a line graph?
questions.explanation: Bars shine for comparing distinct categories side by side.
questions.misconception: Tracking change across time is where line graphs shine — bars are about comparing non-ordered categories.
